title: From patient cells to patient therapy: Twenty years of iPSC-based translation in neurodegenerative disease
abstract: Twenty years after the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells, the field has progressed from patient-specific disease modeling toward cell-based therapies for neurodegenerative disorders. Parkinson's disease has emerged as the leading model for neuronal replacement, whereas Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis require distinct combinations of circuit reconstruction, cellular support, immune modulation, and engineered therapeutic delivery. We discuss key determinants of clinical translation, including cell source, product identity, graft composition, graft-host interactions, manufacturing reproducibility, genomic integrity, and clinical evaluation. We propose that the interval between cell transplantation and long-term engraftment constitutes a biological "black box" in which graft fate and therapeutic outcome are determined. As regenerative medicine enters its third decade, future progress will depend not only on generating therapeutic cells but also on elucidating and engineering the biological processes that determine their fate after transplantation, marking a conceptual transition from stem cell biology toward transplantation biology.

title: Multi-omics-driven personalized management of advanced HCC
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) management is challenging due to its complex tumor microenvironment and poor treatment responses. Here, using tumor specimens from a prospective clinical trial of combined transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), we perform exhaustive multi-omics analysis including spatial proteomics and transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing, and bulk transcriptomics. These analyses reveal that treatment response is associated with enrichment of anti-tumor T cell regions that are regulated by cGAS-STING activation within immune-suppressive epithelial cells. Conversely, fibrotic processes impede these pro-response processes. Based on these insights, we test triple combination therapy consisting of cGAS activation, immune checkpoint blockade, and anti-fibrosis strategies, which shows improved efficacy over dual therapy. To identify patients who would benefit, we construct a predictive model using a group sparse learning algorithm. Our findings provide a blueprint for crafting personalized HCC therapies using next-generation biomarkers.

title: Bridging innate and adaptive immunity: A bispecific SIRPαD1-αPCSK9 fusion protein reprograms macrophages for durable tumor clearance
abstract: T cell priming-thus showing how phagocytosis-targeted therapies can paradoxically suppress adaptive immunity. To overcome this, we engineer bispecific fusion proteins co-targeting the CD47-SIRPα checkpoint and the PCSK9-MHC-I axis, among which SIRPαD1-αPCSK9 is optimal. Dual targeting synergistically enhances phagocytosis, preserves antigen cross-presentation, and reprograms tumor microenvironment toward an immunostimulatory state. Consequently, SIRPαD1-αPCSK9 activates innate and adaptive antitumor immunity, achieving potent tumor control with improved safety. These findings uncover a resistance mechanism to macrophage-centered cancer immunotherapy and establish a dual-targeting strategy bridging phagocytosis and T cell activation.

title: Disruption of the Nav1.8/Ankyrin-3 interaction in nociceptors reduces pathological pain-like behaviors in mice
abstract: Treating chronic neuropathic pain is challenging due to its complex pathophysiology. Persistent changes in the somatosensory system prolong heightened states of stimulus-evoked and spontaneous pain. Nociceptor dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons are key contributors to neuropathic pain due to pathological plasticity following injury, leading to spontaneous ectopic and stimulus-evoked firing. Preclinical strategies to inhibit Nav1.8, a nociceptor-specific voltage-gated sodium channel, are successful in reducing neuropathic pain but have yet to produce similar results in clinical settings. Here, we evaluate the pharmacotherapeutic potential of the Nav1.8/Ank3 interaction in neuropathic pain, utilizing electrophysiology, biochemistry, and proteomic approaches. We report that Nav1.8/Ank3 interactions are necessary for maintaining pathological nociceptor hyperexcitability in neuroma pain and that inhibition of this interaction with a short lipidated peptide (SLiP) is sufficient to alleviate neuropathic pain-like behaviors in mice. This work highlights the value of reevaluating targets for pharmacological intervention to produce analgesia specific to pathological states.

title: Fusion-loop-engineered Zika mRNA vaccine elicits convergent B cell immunodominance to uncouple protection from ADE in macaques
abstract: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) remains a major hurdle for flavivirus vaccine development. Engineering the fusion loop (FL) represents a promising solution, yet validations restricted to murine models limit human translatability due to profound species divergence. Here, we provide a primate-level demonstration that FL-engineered Zika virus (ZIKV)-M/E mRNA vaccination protects against ZIKV challenge with negligible dengue virus (DENV) ADE. The vaccine-induced B cells are overwhelmingly ZIKV specific (>97%), dominated by a convergent population using a germline ortholog of human IGHV5-10-1, a gene preferentially recruited during natural human ZIKV infection. Antibodies derived from this population are highly potent and, mechanistically, achieve multi-stage viral entry blockade. Cryo-electron microscopy analysis reveals that these antibodies target a distinct, vulnerable hotspot on ZIKV. Notably, ZIKV specificity is dictated by the epitope residues D67-M68-A69, whereas a homologous DENV N67-linked glycan imposes steric shielding to preclude cross-reactivity. Our findings demonstrate that FL engineering uncouples protective immunity from ADE for safer human flavivirus vaccines.

title: Oral microbial nitrate metabolism is associated with lower prevalence of prediabetes
abstract: The oral microbiome is a key microbial interface for dietary or oral nitrate metabolism, yet its role in early glycemic dysregulation remains poorly defined. In a population-based cohort ( n = 472), we perform metagenomic profiling of tongue dorsum microbiomes and identify 11 taxa and nine microbial pathways associated with prediabetes. Among these, Rothia mucilaginosa and microbial nitrate reduction emerge as the only taxon and the strongest pathway associated with lower prediabetes prevalence. Individuals without prediabetes show higher salivary nitrate and nitrite concentrations, supporting enhanced oral nitrate bioavailability. Functional characterization of an isolated Rothia mucilaginosa strain demonstrates its capacity to mediate both nitrate-nitrite-NO and nitrate-nitrite-NH 4 + pathways under oxygen-limited conditions. Incorporating nitrate metabolism-associated microbial features into clinical risk factors improves risk stratification for progression to prediabetes. These findings support oral nitrate metabolism as a microbial pathway linking oral ecology to systemic metabolic health and suggest that tongue cleaning may modulate microbial functions involved in this pathway.

title: A translational pipeline for classification of variants of uncertain significance to support gene therapy clinical trial in OTOF-related deafness
abstract: OTOF gene dysfunction causes congenital deafness. OTOF gene therapy achieves promising clinical efficacy. However, OTOF variants of uncertain significance (VUS) hinder diagnosis and restrict eligibility for gene therapy in half of 135 hearing loss patients with biallelic OTOF variants in our cohort. Here, we establish a translational pipeline to reclassify VUSs and guide clinical decisions via functional analysis. We evaluate coding VUSs using an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated variant delivery system into Otof −/− mice and evaluate non-coding VUSs via splicing assays. Isolated homozygous E1700Q confers normal hearing, while E1700Q consistently occurs in cis with K1992R in patients, and K1992R correlates with abnormal otoferlin subcellular localization. This pipeline reclassifies eight representative VUSs, enabling definitive molecular diagnoses for 38 patients. Seven eligible patients receive gene therapy and show auditory improvement, including one achieving near-normal hearing that was sustained for 1.5 years. This pipeline effectively expands the gene therapy eligibility for OTOF -related deafness. This study is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry: ChiCTR2200063181.

title: A standardized patient-derived glioblastoma organoid platform for evaluating radiotherapy efficacy and overcoming resistance
abstract: Patient-derived glioblastoma (GBM) organoids (GBOs) maintain characteristics of their original tumors; however, they have not been widely applied to systematically assess therapy responses at scale or elucidate mechanisms underlying treatment resistance. Here, we develop a standardized reaggregated GBO (rGBO) platform for scalable, quantitative evaluation of radiation responses across 48 patients with GBM. Radiation responses in rGBOs correlate with the survival duration of corresponding patients treated with standard-of-care radiotherapy. Transcriptomic analyses identify gene signatures associated with radiosensitivity and radioresistance. Connectivity mapping with perturbational datasets identifies a panel of compounds with potential for reducing radioresistant and enhancing radiosensitive signatures. Subsequent testing demonstrates that inhibitors of bromodomain and extraterminal (BET) family proteins enhance radiotherapy efficacy in GBO and xenograft models by downregulating the radioresistant signature. Together, our study highlights the potential of rGBOs for standardizing therapeutic screening, evaluating patient-specific responses, identifying associated molecular features, and developing strategies to overcome treatment resistance.

title: Regional brain aging signatures predict mortality through neurovascular immune mechanisms
abstract: Brain aging provides an integrative marker of systemic health, but whether regional patterns outperform whole-brain approaches remains unknown. Here, we show that regional brain age signatures achieve superior mortality prediction through identifiable neurovascular-immune mechanisms in 1,240 community-dwelling adults followed for 10 years (120 deaths). While global brain age independently predicts mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 1.044 per year), a data-driven three-region model combining the left precentral gyrus, left parahippocampal gyrus, and right cerebellum achieves superior discrimination (C-index, 0.81 vs. 0.79, p = 0.032). Integration with plasma proteomics (513 proteins) reveals complement activation and adaptive immune dysregulation as convergent mechanisms. Region-specific vulnerabilities emerge: microvascular dysfunction in the motor cortex, proteostasis failure in the medial temporal structures, and iron dysregulation in the cerebellum. Longitudinal imaging (n = 444) identifies accelerated brain aging phenotypes predicting cognitive decline (HR, 1.558; p = 0.042). These findings establish regional neuroimaging-proteomic integration as a precision strategy linking network-specific vulnerabilities to systemic immune processes.

title: Lipid-engineered antibody-based therapeutics target inflamed joints and lymph nodes to enhance rheumatoid arthritis treatment
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammation and joint damage. Although antibody (Ab)-based biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) have transformed RA treatment, their efficacy remains limited in many patients. Here, we conjugate Ab-based bDMARDs with pegylated diacyllipid (DP) motifs to enable their albumin hitchhiking after subcutaneous administration, thereby targeting these lipid-drug conjugates (LDCs) to both inflamed joints and lymph nodes (LNs) for enhanced and concurrent immunosuppression. Multivalent DP conjugation allows bDMARDs larger than albumin to engage multiple albumin molecules, further enhancing albumin-mediated targeting. In a collagen-induced arthritis model, DP modification substantially improves the therapeutic efficacy of two representative bDMARDs, TNF-α-neutralizing Ab (aTNF-α) and CTLA4-immunoglobin recombinant protein (CTLA4), without detectable additional safety risks. bDMARDs bearing two DP moieties significantly outperform their single-DP-modified counterparts, consistent with more extensive albumin engagement. LDC offers a potent, facile, and broadly applicable strategy for targeting Ab-based therapeutics to inflamed tissues and LNs.

title: Prognostic value of cfDNA methylation in locally advanced esophageal squamous cell cancer treated with neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy
abstract: We prospectively evaluated whether longitudinal cfDNA methylation predicts pathological complete response (pCR) and survival in 70 patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) receiving neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy. Serial plasma samples (n = 183) were collected at four time points: pre-neoadjuvant treatment (NAT), post-NAT, pre-surgery, and post-surgery. Targeted whole-genome cfDNA methylation sequencing was performed, and cancer detection (CD) values were calculated with positivity, defined as CD ≥ 0.7. CD positivity dropped from 74% pre-NAT to 31% post-NAT (p < 0.001). Pre-surgery CD positivity was significantly higher in non-pCR versus pCR patients (33% vs. 0%; p = 0.028). A model incorporating post-NAT CD value and clinical factors achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.764 for pCR. Post-NAT CD-negative patients had significantly improved disease-free survival (DFS; hazard ratio [HR] = 0.33; p = 0.035). Findings were reproduced in an expanded 30-patient cohort. Dynamic cfDNA methylation monitoring is associated with pCR and DFS, warranting further validation in larger cohorts.

title: A spatiotemporal atlas of radiation-induced brain injury reveals dysfunction of the blood-CSF barrier
abstract: Radiotherapy for brain tumors frequently induces irreversible cognitive decline, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we present an integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlas of radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) in mice, spanning the acute to chronic phases. We reveal that the early-delayed phase following irradiation represents a critical window during which the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier (BCSFB) integrity is compromised. This disruption results from the selective depletion of a radiosensitive Tmsb4x + epithelial subpopulation in the choroid plexus, which functions as a gatekeeper for the BCSFB. Consequently, CSF-derived macrophages excessively infiltrate the periventricular niche and engage in spatial crosstalk with interferon-responsive microglia. This dysregulated immune axis sustains chronic neuroinflammation, driving the late-stage neurodegeneration and cognitive impairment. In conclusion, our study establishes a high-resolution spatiotemporal framework and positions the BCSFB as a pivotal immune gateway and a promising therapeutic target for mitigating RIBI.

title: Reviving low-affinity glycan-targeting CAR with combinatorial design
abstract: CD19CAR T cells demonstrate remarkable therapeutic efficacy in the treatment of B cell malignancies. A global limitation of conventional CD19CAR therapy is its mono-specificity. Thus, defining complementary targets to CD19 is critical to avoid target-dependent limitations. Alternatives to protein antigens include secondary modifications, such as glycosylation. One example of aberrant glycosylation in lymphoma is the increase in N-glycans capped with α2,6-linked sialic acid, named CD75s. Here, we generate a CAR that recognizes CD75s based on an IgM monoclonal antibody called HH2. HH2CAR shows cytotoxic activity against B cell lymphoma cell lines, although it induces little to no cytokine release. However, while HH2CAR alone cannot control tumor progression in vivo, its combination with CD19CAR results in a functional molecule. Beyond overcoming the limited efficiency of HH2CAR T cells, this combination also prevents potential off-tumor/on-target toxicity associated with CD19 single targeting. Thus, inefficient mono-specific CAR molecules can be effectively leveraged in combinatorial formats.

title: Human genetic evidence challenges NCOA1 as a monogenic obesity gene
abstract: Obesity is a heterogeneous disease with a substantial genetic component. Rare pathogenic variants in genes of the leptin-melanocortin pathway can cause monogenic obesity and support targeted therapies such as setmelanotide, a melanocortin 4 receptor agonist. Pathogenic variants in NCOA1, encoding the nuclear receptor co-activator SRC-1, have recently been proposed as a cause of monogenic obesity through impaired leptin-induced POMC activation, leading to the inclusion of NCOA1 variant carriers in the EMANATE setmelanotide trial. However, despite biological rationale, the contribution of NCOA1 variants to human obesity remains elusive. Here, we assess NCOA1 variants with case-control analyses in adults and children from the RaDiO study, combined with in vitro assays and replication in the UK Biobank. We find no association between pathogenic NCOA1 variants and obesity or body mass index.

title: Microbiota-mediated naringenin release limits postoperative acute gastrointestinal injury by suppressing ferroptosis
abstract: Acute gastrointestinal injury (AGI) remains a major complication after cardiopulmonary bypass, yet its microbiome-related determinants are unclear. We identify microbiota-mediated naringenin (NAR) release as a candidate modulator of AGI susceptibility. Patients who subsequently develop AGI have lower preoperative fecal NAR levels and β-glucuronidase (GUS) activity, accompanied by reduced abundance of Bacteroides vulgatus (B. vulgatus). In germ-free and conventional mice, B. vulgatus alleviates intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury through GUS-dependent release of NAR from its glucuronide conjugate. Mechanistically, NAR engages the TLR4/MyD88-SPRR2A axis to suppress CHAC1-driven ferroptosis, thereby maintaining epithelial integrity and promoting mucosal repair in vivo and in organoids. Clinically, preoperative fecal NAR concentration and GUS activity show exploratory value as noninvasive markers for postoperative AGI risk stratification. Collectively, these findings support a microbiota-host metabolic model in which microbial NAR release may mitigate postoperative gastrointestinal injury by restricting ferroptosis, with potential implications for risk assessment and therapeutic modulation.

title: Microbiota-regulated TCDCA associates with Parkinson’s disease severity and promotes BBB dysfunction through VSMC TGR5 signaling in mice
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a systemic disorder linked to gut dysbiosis, yet key microbiota-regulated metabolites remain unclear. Here, we observe elevated taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) in patients with PD that correlates with disease severity. Reduced bile salt hydrolase (BSH) gene abundance correlates inversely with circulating TCDCA, consistent with altered bile acid deconjugation. Exogenous TCDCA correlates with aggravated motor and gastrointestinal deficits, impaired blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and accelerated dopaminergic neurodegeneration in a PD mouse model. Mechanistically, TCDCA links to TGR5 signaling activation in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), alongside PKCα-dependent mitochondrial apoptosis and BBB disruption. VSMC-specific Tgr5 deletion coincides with neurovascular protection. Supplementation with a BSH-high Lactobacillus reuteri strain reduces TCDCA concentrations, improves gut and BBB integrity, mitigates inflammation, and alleviates PD-like phenotypes in a BSH-dependent manner. These data support a gut-BBB-brain axis linked to PD, identifying TCDCA as a candidate pathological marker.

title: Anti-HDGFL2 cryptic protein antibodies provide a sensitive readout of TDP-43 pathology and clinical disease features
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein (TDP-43) cytoplasmic aggregates and nuclear depletion contribute to TDP-43 dysfunction in frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP) and forms of motor neuron disease (MND), particularly amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). TDP-43 regulates alternative splicing, but its dysfunction can engender the inclusion of cryptic exons (CEs) during splicing. Transcripts harboring an in-frame CE can generate de novo proteins. One example is the CE variant of hepatoma-derived growth factor-like protein 2 (HDGFL2-CE). To understand HDGFL2-CE as a readout of TDP-43 dysfunction, and its spatial relationship with TDP-43 pathology, we generate anti-HDGFL2-CE polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies and develop sensitive HDGFL2-CE immunoassays. With these tools, we observe that HDGFL2-CE accumulates in neurons with TDP-43 pathology, and that higher frontal cortex HDGFL2-CE in FTLD-TDP and FTLD-TDP/MND associates with greater pathological TDP-43, earlier age of onset, and shorter survival, supporting HDGFL2-CE as a marker tightly linked to TDP-43 dysfunction and clinical disease features.

title: AI-integrated RNA therapeutics in precision oncology
abstract: RNA therapeutics can silence oncogenic transcripts, modulate RNA processing, restore protein expression, or encode tumor antigens. Their development, however, is constrained by target selection, molecular design, delivery, immunogenicity, and inter-patient heterogeneity. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to these bottlenecks through multi-omics target prioritization, RNA structure and sequence modeling, delivery optimization, neoantigen selection, patient stratification, and manufacturing quality control. The maturity of these applications is uneven: within oncology, messenger RNA (mRNA) cancer vaccines are the most clinically advanced RNA-based strategy, whereas therapeutic approaches involving long non-coding RNAs and circular RNAs remain predominantly preclinical or early clinical, and most AI-enabled methods lack prospective clinical validation. In this review, we evaluate AI across the RNA therapeutic development pipeline, distinguish evidence-supported applications from preclinical and speculative uses, and discuss the validation, regulatory, and data-governance requirements for translation into precision oncology.

title: Breastfeeding and maternal microbial reservoirs are associated with infant gut phageome development during the first year of life
abstract: The early-life assembly of the gut microbiome is a critical determinant of long-term health, yet the role of bacteriophages in this process remains poorly understood. Here we longitudinally profile the gut phageome of 34 mother-infant dyads during the first year of life with metagenomics and a phage-centered computational workflow. Phage diversity increases with age, paralleling bacterial diversification but following distinct ecological trajectories. Shared viral populations across maternal and infant samples are consistent with potential maternal contribution, although not indicative of direct transmission. Feeding-related variables are consistently associated with phageome composition at specific developmental stages. No single factor fully explains phageome variation, supporting a multifactorial model involving maternal, environmental, and dietary inputs. Together, these findings provide a framework for understanding early-life phage ecology, positioning phages as active participants in early microbiome assembly and supporting the inclusion of viral components in microbiome-based strategies aimed at promoting healthy ecosystem development in infancy.

title: Spatially tuned localization of interleukins and OX40 agonists enhances synergistic anti-tumor immunity
abstract: Abstract Advances in immunotherapy have revolutionized the current standard of care for cancer patients, but unfortunately, most approaches still fail to mount a robust anti-cancer effect. This is in part due to a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment which has developed bio-orthogonal mechanisms of immune escape. To address this challenge, the field has turned to combination immunotherapies, but systemic administration of potent combination therapies has resulted in severe immune related adverse effects and toxicity. Enabling potent combination immunotherapies requires administering these immune agonists in a way that more closely resembles the endogenous cancer immunity cycle, a tightly regulated sequence of cues in both space and time. Here, we explore the ability of an injectable hydrogel depot to enable the rational localization of potent immunotherapeutic cytokines (IL-12, IL-2) and antibodies (OX40a). We hypothesized that selectively altering the biodistribution of these cargo would enable tolerable and synergic anti-cancer combinations, so we leveraged a previously characterized injectable polymer-nanoparticle (PNP) hydrogel system to deliver these agonists either intratumorally (IT) or peritumorally (PT). Using in vivo imaging, we demonstrated that site of administration is critical to redistributing cargo to either the tumor or tumor draining lymph node (tdLN). Further, we demonstrated that the targeted localization of cytokine and antibody therapies synergistically improved treatment efficacy in the B16F10 and MC38 tumor models and altered cellular phenotypes in these microenvironments. This approach thus represents a crucial new strategy for basic cancer immunology and materials-based immuno-engineering research while improving therapeutic efficacy.

title: Orally delivered metabolically reprogrammed probiotics for cascade-activated antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer
abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) remains limited due to the inherently low tumor immunogenicity and the profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Herein, capitalizing on the metabolic traits and anatomical accessibility of CRC, we propose a broadly applicable oral strategy based on metabolically engineered bacteria (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for CRC immunotherapy. Mechanistically, cystathionine γ-lyase expressed by EHC disrupts redox homeostasis, triggering ferroptosis in CRC cells and thereby enhancing tumor immunogenicity. Concurrently, the intrinsic adjuvant activity of the bacteria amplifies the cancer-immunity cycle driven by immunogenic cell death and remodels the immunosuppressive TME. In vivo studies demonstrate that this orally delivered engineered bacterial platform not only suppresses the growth of orthotopic CRC tumors but also inhibits metastatic progression, indicating the induction of a potent systemic immune response. Immune profiling confirms robust systemic and gut mucosal immune activation following oral administration. Collectively, this oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform is precisely tailored to the features of CRC and offers a safe and effective immunotherapeutic strategy for this malignancy.

title: Safety and efficacy of high-current tTIS targeting left sgACC for major depressive disorder: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability, and non-invasive stimulation of deep brain circuits such as the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) remains challenging. This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial recruits 96 adults with moderate-to-severe MDD who received 10 sessions of 2 mA low-current, 15 mA high-current, or sham transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) targeting the left sgACC. The high-current group shows significantly greater reductions in depressive symptoms (17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale [HDRS-17] score) post-treatment and at 1-month follow-up compared with sham and outperforms the low-current group post-treatment. Exploratory Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) analyses suggest improved sleep quality in both active groups, whereas anxiety outcomes show no intergroup differences. High-current tTIS is safe and well tolerated, with only transient tingling. These findings provide preliminary evidence that sgACC-targeted tTIS relieves depressive symptoms safely, with more robust short-to medium-term effects observed under the 15 mA protocol. This trial registers on Chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2400094971).

title: Prediction of immunotherapy response using live tumor fragments from routine clinical biopsies
abstract: Functional ex vivo assays using live tumor tissues have demonstrated strong predictive accuracy for response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) but are not scalable, requiring manual processing of large resections collected at academic centers. Here, an ex vivo live tumor fragment platform was developed using standard-of-care biopsies from 228 patients with suspected malignancy across prospective, multicenter observational studies. Hierarchical clustering of changes in cytokine production between an IgG baseline phase and an ICI treatment phase identified two clusters: heatmap responder and nonresponder. A binary classifier (elive index) using eight cytokines achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.99 for heatmap cluster prediction. elive index aligned with clinical benefit in 93% (26/28) of patients ( p = 3.2 × 10 −5 ) and identified 83% (10/12) of objective responders. elive responders were found among biomarker-negative patients, highlighting the platform as a scalable approach that may complement existing companion diagnostics. This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05478538, NCT05520099, NCT06349642, and NCT07327489).

title: NKG2D overexpression potentiates CAR-T cells through costimulation by tumor NKG2D ligands
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable success in hematologic malignancies, but durable efficacy remains limited by insufficient CAR-T cell persistence. Here, we show that activated CAR-T cells upregulate multiple NKG2D ligands (NKG2DLs), increasing their susceptibility to natural killer (NK) cell-mediated CAR-T cell cytotoxicity. To address this vulnerability, we engineer CAR-T cells to overexpress full-length NKG2D (CAR-NG). NKG2D overexpression reduces the surface accessibility of endogenous NKG2DLs without decreasing their total protein abundance. In parallel, engagement of tumor-expressed NKG2DLs in trans provides additional costimulatory signals, enhancing CAR-T cell activation and proliferation while attenuating exhaustion-associated phenotypes. In hematologic and solid tumor models, CAR-NG cells exhibit reduced susceptibility to NK-cell-mediated cytotoxicity, improved tumor control, increased in vivo expansion, deeper tumor infiltration, and no evident additional toxicity compared with conventional CAR-T cells. These findings identify NKG2D overexpression as an engineering strategy that enhances CAR-T antitumor activity primarily through tumor NKG2DL-dependent trans costimulation.

title: Targeting MMGT1 enhances immunotherapy efficacy in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: The role of senescent tumor cells in modulating the immune microenvironment and influencing immunotherapy efficacy remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the function of the senescence-associated gene membrane magnesium transporter 1 (MMGT1) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) immunotherapy. MMGT1 is upregulated in TNBC and correlates with poor prognosis. Mammary gland-specific knockout of Mmgt1 significantly impedes tumor growth. Mechanistically, MMGT1 promotes lipid metabolism by facilitating translocation of the SCAP-SREBP1 complex to the Golgi apparatus, thereby suppressing cellular senescence. Notably, senescent TNBC cells enhance CD8 + T cell proliferation and cytotoxicity through CCL20 secretion. Furthermore, a positive feedback loop exists between MMGT1 and SREBP1. In vivo , AZ191 downregulates MMGT1 expression, which suppresses tumor growth and enhances the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy. Collectively, these findings reveal a critical role for MMGT1 in shaping the TNBC immune microenvironment and suggest that targeting MMGT1 represents a promising strategy to improve anti-PD-1 immunotherapy outcomes.

title: Targeting oncogenic SOX2 condensates suppresses squamous cell carcinoma progression
abstract: Squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) comprise a group of lethal malignancies, yet developing SCC-specific therapies remains challenging, largely due to a lack of druggable targets. We identify SOX2 condensation as a shared cancer hallmark across esophageal, head and neck, and lung SCCs. Within SOX2, the activation domain 1 (AD1) acts as the condensate-promoting region via its aromatic and hydrophobic residues. Site-specific mutagenesis, orthotopic mouse models, and multi-omics sequencing demonstrate that SOX2 condensates upregulate oncogene expression by enhancing SOX2 chromatin occupancy, H3K27ac enrichment, and chromatin interactions at oncogenic loci such as FGFR2, thereby promoting SCC progression. An FDA-approved drug screen reveals that the proteasome inhibitor ixazomib disrupts SOX2 condensates in an HSP70-dependent manner. Upon ixazomib treatment, the substrate-binding domain of HSP70 blocks SOX2 AD1, selectively dissolving SOX2 condensates, downregulating oncogene expression, and suppressing condensate-positive SCC patient-derived xenografts. These findings highlight targeting SOX2 condensates with proteasome inhibitors as an SCC-specific, biomarker-guided therapeutic strategy.

title: Isobavachalcone targets deubiquitinase OTUB1 to induce PD-L1 degradation and enhances antitumor immunity
abstract: PD-L1-mediated immunosuppression is a key mechanism underlying tumor immune evasion, whereas PD-1/PD-L1 blockade therapies remain limited by low response rates and acquired resistance. Through small-molecule screening, we identify isobavachalcone (IBC), a naturally derived compound that modulates PD-L1 homeostasis by targeting the deubiquitinase OTUB1. Mechanistically, IBC targets OTUB1 at the His217 residue and suppresses its deubiquitinase activity, thereby promoting K48-linked polyubiquitination of PD-L1 and its proteasome-dependent degradation. Functionally, IBC reduces tumor cell PD-L1 expression and enhances CD8 + T cell-mediated cytotoxicity. In PD-L1-deficient tumor models, IBC fails to further enhance antitumor activity, indicating that PD-L1 is required for IBC-mediated immune regulation. Moreover, IBC combined with anti-CTLA-4 therapy further enhanced antitumor efficacy. Together, these findings highlight IBC as a potential drug candidate that promotes PD-L1 degradation and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of targeting the OTUB1-PD-L1 axis to improve immune checkpoint therapy.

title: Gut-derived glucagon-like peptides attenuate T cell-induced intestinal injury
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) are produced in enteroendocrine L cells and control energy homeostasis. GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) activation improves glucose homeostasis and induces satiety and weight loss, whereas GLP-2 receptor (GLP-2R) signaling promotes intestinal growth and nutrient absorption. GLP-1R and GLP-2R agonism also reduce intestinal damage in preclinical studies. Here, we demonstrate that endogenous GLP-1R and GLP-2R signaling are essential for protecting the intestine from T cell-mediated enteropathy. Gut injury induced by T cell activation is increased in Glp1r −/− and Glp2r −/− mice, as well as in mice with selective loss of intestinal proglucagon gene expression ( Gcg Gut−/− ). Conversely, the GLP-2R agonist teduglutide and the GLP-1R agonist semaglutide, administered separately or together, attenuate αCD3-induced intestinal damage in Gcg Gut−/− mice. Collectively, these findings demonstrate distinct biological roles for endogenous GLP-1R/GLP-2R activity in immune-mediated intestinal injury and highlight the therapeutic potential of glucagon-like peptides, alone or together, for ameliorating T cell-mediated mucosal injury.

title: The next click in antibody drug conjugate development
abstract: The clinical success of antibody drug conjugates has been shaped by the promise of delivering cytotoxic payloads precisely to tumors while minimizing systemic exposure. Simó and colleagues aim to improve on conventional ADC delivery by decoupling tumor localization from payload delivery to enhance pharmacokinetics and addressing antigen heterogeneity by enabling dual targeting.

title: CD47 fuels intestinal fibrosis by inducing fibroblast phagocytic evasion and represents a therapeutic target
abstract: Intestinal fibrosis is a major complication of Crohn's disease, for which targeted therapies remain unavailable. Fibrosis is defined by excess matrix deposition, which may result from inadequate phagocytic clearance, yet how phagocytosis shifts here is unclear. Using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we identify fibrosis-associated CD47 hi fibroblasts coupled to SIRPA hi macrophages in fibrotic regions. Cell-cell communication analyses and neutralizing-antibody experiments identify interleukin-1β as a mediator of their crosstalk, forming a profibrotic niche characterized by phagocytic evasion. Genetic disruption of fibroblast Cd47 or macrophage Sirpa enhances fibroblast clearance and attenuates fibrosis. Mechanistically, checkpoint disruption reprograms macrophages toward an NRF2-associated pro-phagocytic state, linking enhanced clearance to the antifibrotic response. Furthermore, therapeutic antibody blockade of this checkpoint attenuates intestinal fibrosis in mouse models with schedule-dependent efficacy. Collectively, these findings support CD47-mediated phagocytic evasion as a key pathogenic mechanism in intestinal fibrosis and identify CD47-SIRPα blockade as a promising therapeutic target.

title: 20 years of iPSCs: From cellular reprogramming to clinical translation
abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) were first generated in 2006 by Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi at Kyoto University. Their landmark work demonstrated that mature somatic cells could be reprogrammed to a pluripotent state through the expression of four transcription factors, now known as the Yamanaka factors. In 2012, Dr. Yamanaka and Sir John B. Gurdon were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning reprogramming mature cells to make them pluripotent.

title: Inhibition of the CTP synthase 1 prevents GVHD and delays skin graft rejection revealing distinct alloreactive T cell responses
abstract: Acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD), following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and organ rejection are serious immune-mediated complications driven by alloreactive T cells. CTPS1, a crucial enzyme for de novo CTP synthesis, is essential for the proliferation of activated T cells, representing an attractive therapeutic target for controlling T cell-mediated pathologies. In this study, using Ctps1-deficient T cells in fully MHC-mismatched and haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation models, a complete blockage in the induction of aGVHD is observed in association with significantly reduced alloreactive effector T cell expansion. In skin graft rejection models, expansion of alloreactive Ctps1-deficient T cells is reduced, and graft destruction is delayed but not prevented. Notably, the healing process allows T cells to mediate skin graft rejection independently of CTPS1. Finally, treatment with a specific CTPS1 inhibitor rescues mice from lethal aGVHD. Our results underscore the pivotal role of CTPS1 in driving alloreactive T cell responses, highlighting its potential for aGVHD treatment.

title: CNS targeted AAV gene therapies: Recent advances and clinical insights
abstract: Adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors are currently the leading platform for in vivo gene transfer to the central nervous system (CNS). Eight FDA-approved AAV therapies, including four for CNS disorders, demonstrate that AAV-based genetic medicines can alter the course of devastating neurological diseases. At the same time, preclinical and clinical experience has identified persistent and interdependent barriers, including dose-dependent toxicities, off-target transduction, and the ∼4.7 kb packaging limit that must be addressed for broader clinical impact and continued success. Here, we review AAV biology and recent capsid engineering strategies, assess how route of administration and packaging constraints impact safety and efficacy, and synthesize clinical and postmarketing data from both CNS and non-CNS AAV gene therapies. We conclude that no single capsid, route of delivery, or expression strategy will address all CNS disorders, and that safe and efficacious treatment will require optimization of capsid, cargo, and administration on a disease-by-disease basis.

title: Targeted lactate depletion via gluconeogenesis by engineered hepatocyte-based micronanorobots for radiosensitization and immune activation
abstract: Radiotherapy is often limited by tumor-intrinsic DNA repair and an immunosuppressive microenvironment, both of which are reinforced by lactate accumulation. Here, we develop a CXCR4-engineered enucleated hepatocyte cytoplast platform decorated with Au-Pt Janus nanorobots (AP/LC CXCR4 ) to deplete intratumoral lactate and amplify radiation-induced oxidative stress. The hepatocyte cytoplasts home to tumors and consume lactate through gluconeogenesis, reducing repair-associated protein lactylation and impairing MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) co-fractionation and chromatin recruitment, thereby impairing double-strand break repair. In parallel, the Au-Pt nanorobots enhance reactive oxygen species generation under acidic tumor conditions, increasing radiation damage. In radioresistant colorectal cancer models and a metastatic cervical cancer model, AP/LC CXCR4 combined with radiotherapy sustains DNA damage, promotes immunogenic cell death, reduces immunosuppressive myeloid and regulatory T (Treg) cell populations, enhances dendritic cell maturation and CD8 + T cell activation, and improves tumor control and survival.

title: Tumor digital twins uncover therapeutic strategies in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options and a high risk of relapse and mortality. Consequently, there is a critical need for personalized treatment strategies that reflect the unique biology, clonal architecture, and evolutionary dynamics of individual tumors. Here, we present a TNBC digital twin framework, built from prior knowledge and formulated as a mechanistic qualitative network in which nodes represent genes and proteins and edges denote the interactions between them. Parameterized with patient-specific molecular data, the model identifies potential resistance mechanisms and proposes tailored treatment plans to overcome them. We validate the model using clinical data from PARTNER, a large, randomized controlled trial evaluating platinum-based chemotherapy with or without PARP inhibitors. The model accurately predicts treatment responses and identifies mutational and transcriptional biomarkers associated with clinical outcome. Our approach offers an interpretable alternative to black-box predictive models, enabling transparent decision-making in precision oncology.

title: An in vivo T cell engager platform induces deep plasma cell depletion in autoimmune dry eye
abstract: Abstract Bispecific T cell engagers (TCEs) have transformed targeted immunotherapy but remain constrained by ex vivo manufacturing and systemic delivery, limiting their application in autoimmune disorders. Here, we introduce the first in vivo TCE platform, utilizing a T cell-targeted integration-deficient lentiviral vector (T-IDLE) to reprogram endogenous T cells into engineered T cells secreting BCMA×CD3 TCEs (STCEs) directly in vivo . In murine Sjögren’s syndrome-associated dry eye model, a single intravenous administration of T-IDLE STCE achieved deep and sustained depletion of plasmablasts and plasma cells, reversing lacrimal gland inflammation and restoring tear production without detectable off-target transduction. Longitudinal studies in cynomolgus monkeys confirmed translational promise, demonstrating potent plasma cell clearance and favorable safety profiles over 12 weeks post-vector dosing. Mechanistic analyses demonstrated attenuation of Th1/Th17-mediated inflammation and controlled cytokine responses, accompanied by negligible vector integration in non-T cell lineages, thereby substantiating the safety profile of the integration-deficient design. This first-in-class in vivo TCE approach represents a manufacturing-free, scalable immunotherapy strategy for autoantibody-mediated diseases.

title: Moving beyond overconfidence: A clinical roadmap for integrating uncertainty-aware AI models into medical workflows
abstract: Conventional artificial intelligence (AI) models can remain overconfident when their predictions are unreliable, limiting clinical adoption. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) supplements predictions with information about confidence, but the literature is often mathematically dense and difficult to translate into action. In this clinically oriented review, we synthesize current evidence and offer a practical perspective on the deployment of uncertainty-aware AI. We describe how uncertainty arises, summarize four principal computational approaches, and examine applications across clinical tasks, model development, foundation models, large language models, and agentic workflows. Uncertainty estimates may identify outputs requiring review, but they do not independently establish safety; their value depends on validation against relevant errors and linkage to appropriate actions in the intended setting. We, therefore, propose an adaptable roadmap connecting local reliability evaluation and threshold selection with subgroup assessment, prospective clinical evaluation, ongoing monitoring, and governance.

title: Interpretable deep learning maps spatial morphological phenotypes to HCC and LUAD survival
abstract: The clinical adoption of deep learning in pathology is largely hindered by the "black box" nature of current models, which often obscure the biological basis of prognosis. Here, we introduce MorphX, an interpretable framework that predicts patient survival by explicitly decoding multi-scale morphological patterns from whole-slide images. Unlike conventional methods relying on latent features, MorphX fuses macro-scale tissue texture with micro-scale nuclear metrics to attribute risk to interpretable biological phenotypes. In a multi-center study spanning 1,067 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), MorphX achieves concordance indices of 0.775-0.799 in discovery cohorts. Crucially, we derive eight distinct morphology-based biomarkers-driven by texture heterogeneity in necrotic regions, lymphocyte density, and nuclear shape-that demonstrate reproducible survival associations across independent cohorts, offering a granular resolution of tumor aggressiveness that transcends traditional histological grading. By translating opaque computational predictions into validated biological insights, MorphX supports trustworthy, transparent, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven precision oncology.

title: Engineered receptor-biased IL-2–drug immunoconjugates selectively expand Tregs and suppress effector cells for autoimmune therapy
abstract: Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases arise from a breakdown of immune tolerance driven by hyperactivation of effector lymphocytes and dysfunction of regulatory T (Treg) cells. Interleukin-2 (IL-2) supports both Treg maintenance and effector cell responses, necessitating careful dose optimization for selective immune regulation. Here, we report an immunoconjugate strategy that integrates Treg-selective cytokine signaling with localized pharmacological suppression by coupling a site-specifically PEGylated IL-2 variant (Y31-20K) to immunosuppressive small molecules. Through systematic screening, we identify Y31-20K-KU as the lead construct, which restores immune homeostasis in patient-derived lymphocytes and ameliorates pathology in mouse models of chronic colitis and collagen-induced arthritis. Mechanistically, Y31-20K-KU selectively expands Tregs while concurrently suppressing effector cells and exhibited favorable safety with minimal immunogenicity, thereby overcoming limitations of cytokine- and small-molecule-based monotherapies. These findings establish IL-2–drug immunoconjugates as a clinically tractable strategy for bidirectional immune modulation, providing a versatile platform for reprogramming cytokine signaling in inflammatory diseases.

title: Voices on programmed cell death: From pathways to therapy
abstract: To coincide with the Cell Press Symposium "Taking programmed cell death from mechanisms to interventions," we highlight different viewpoints on challenges and future directions for translating programmed cell death mechanisms into effective therapies.

title: An integrated breast cancer transcriptomic atlas defines clinical subtypes and informs cellular origin
abstract: Efforts to analyze breast cancer transcriptomes at scale are hindered by cross-study technical variability. To overcome this challenge, we adapt single-cell RNA sequencing analytical strategies to harmonize 7,612 bulk breast cancer transcriptomes from 22 datasets, generating a high-resolution atlas that resolves both established and unrecognized malignant transcriptional states. This framework recapitulates intrinsic subtypes and microenvironmental programs while identifying stem-like, basal-luminal progenitor (BLP), mucinous, and neuroendocrine-differentiated (NED) subtypes with distinct clinical behaviors. The NED subtype exhibits luminal characteristics, neuroendocrine differentiation, and poor prognosis after chemo-endocrine therapy. The human epithelial growth factor receptor-2-enriched (HER2E) kinase inhibitor-sensitive (HER2E KIS ) subtype identifies patients who responded to neoadjuvant HER2-targeted kinase inhibition. Transcriptomic positioning of BLP tumors suggests bipotent or myoepithelial progenitor association, unfavorable prognosis after chemotherapy, and potential benefit from VEGF and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Together, these data indicate that this atlas refines breast cancer taxonomy, provides insight into tumor cell states and origins, and establishes a framework for patient stratification and therapeutic discovery.
